title: The calendar, again
tomorrow: what's a shepherd with a flute doing on a big book's cover?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bakhita found a different master, and the modern saints came back: saints of our time. Today, where all those saints live: the calendar.
screen: `SAINTS OF OUR TIME.` → `WHERE THEY ALL LIVE.`

segments.voice: Open the calendar on your phone and it's full of birthdays you forgot you saved. The Church's calendar is fuller still. Its book of saints, the Roman Martyrology, names someone to remember on every day of the year. So is that too much, or exactly right? Inside the Church, there are two honest answers, and each one has a real case.
screen: `BIRTHDAYS YOU FORGOT YOU SAVED.` → `SOMEONE ON EVERY DAY.` → `TOO MUCH, OR EXACTLY RIGHT?`

segments.voice: One side says: Christ's own story comes first. The Second Vatican Council asked that the feasts of the saints not take the place of the feasts that celebrate salvation itself: Christmas, Easter, the Sundays and the seasons. It suggested that many saints be kept by a single country, diocese or religious order, rather than by the whole Church. So the calendar for everyone was trimmed. On this view, a year packed with saints can bury the story they all point to. The other side says: every day, someone. The Martyrology is still read, day by day, in many monasteries. Families keep name days, parishes keep their patrons, and a teenager can find the saint born in her own century on her own birthday. The Catechism says that when the Church remembers the martyrs and saints, it proclaims the paschal mystery in them: Christ's death and rising, lived out in a person. On this view, the saints don't crowd the story. They are the story, told in face after face. Here's the one to tell a friend: the same council document that trimmed the calendar also says the feasts of the saints proclaim the wonderful works of Christ in his servants. Both sides want Christ at the center. One clears space around him. The other finds him in a different face each morning. Scripture keeps a line for both: "All things have their season."
screen: `ONE SIDE: CHRIST'S STORY FIRST.` · `THE OTHER: EVERY DAY, A FACE.` · `BOTH WANT CHRIST AT THE CENTER.` · `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.` · then, large: `EVERY DAY, SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Write tomorrow's date by hand on a scrap of paper, and leave a space beside it for a name. If you already know a saint the Church remembers tomorrow, write the name in; if not, the blank is fine, a small question waiting for the morning.
The calendar. The Church's year: Christ's seasons first, and a saint remembered on every day.
Pocket this one: every day, someone, and every one of them pointing back to the same Christ. Good night.

howItsDone: Catholics follow the liturgical year of seasons and Sundays, and keep memorials of saints through it; many monasteries read the day's entry from the Roman Martyrology, and families celebrate name days and patron saints.

chat.says: Mia saw my app has a saint for every day. she said "isn't Sunday enough?" what do i tell her?
options: Some Catholics agree: Sunday and the seasons come first. Others love a saint a day.
Every saint's day is a holy day, so Catholics go to Mass every single day.
Sunday doesn't matter much anymore; the saints' days are what really count.
chat.meaning: The council put Christ's feasts and seasons first and kept a saint for each day inside them. Both views are Catholic, and both point to Christ.

Roman Martyrology.meaning: the Church's book of saints remembered on each day

Second Vatican Council.meaning: a gathering of the world's bishops that renewed Catholic worship

diocese.meaning: a local church led by a bishop

paschal mystery.meaning: Christ's death and rising, at the heart of Catholic faith

name days.meaning: the feast of the saint whose name you share

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy

notes: Ecclesiastes 3:1 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner): 'All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven.' Confirm.

Sacrosanctum Concilium 111 paraphrased twice: saints' feasts must not take precedence over the feasts of the mysteries of salvation; many may be left to a particular Church, nation or religious family; the feasts of the saints proclaim the wonderful works of Christ in his servants. Confirm.
'the calendar for everyone was trimmed' refers to the post-conciliar revision of the General Roman Calendar; confirm the phrasing.
'names someone to remember on every day of the year' (the Roman Martyrology) and 'still read, day by day, in many monasteries': confirm both (the second is a 'many' claim).
Myth: only a few days carry the Mass obligation (CCC 2177, 2180 and national norms); confirm the wording 'most are memorials'.
Debate day: both views are Catholic and given without a verdict; the shared point (Christ at the center) is from SC 111 and CCC 1173.
